title: Was the Eiffel Tower Almost Torn Down in 1909?
description:
People online often say the Eiffel Tower was "almost torn down in 1909." This episode tells only what the records show. On January 8, 1887, the State, the City of Paris and Eiffel signed a contract: Eiffel got 1.5 million francs plus the operating rights for the Exposition year and for twenty years from January 1, 1890. Once the Exposition ended, the tower belonged to the City of Paris; what went back at the end of the term was the operating rights, and the contract had no clause to demolish it then. On February 14, 1887, Le Temps printed the artists' protest; in an interview the same day Eiffel said that after the term the tower would belong to the city, which could "do with it as it pleases," and that in wartime it could keep Paris connected with the rest of France. In 1898 Ducretet sent wireless signals from the tower to the Panthéon. In 1903 the Prefect of the Seine asked the tower's supervisory commission "keep or demolish?", and it voted unanimously to keep it. In 1906 a city council committee report wrote "Keep it, or tear it down?" and left the decision to its successors; the council first extended the term five years, to 1915. In 1908 the War Ministry called the tower "the only antenna support of its kind in the world," and the rights were extended eleven more years, to 1926. In late January 1910 the Seine flood swamped the underground radio station near the tower; on May 23 the tower sent its first public time signal.

Limits: we found no plan, proposal or vote to demolish the tower. The 1906 line "Keep it, or tear it down?" comes from a committee report quoted in Morice's 1936 law thesis; we did not open the original. We found no "70-year renewal in 1910": the French Court of Audit's 1953-1954 report lists extensions in 1906 and 1908, a twenty-year extension under the contract for World War I, and a 1946 agreement extending to 1980. The 1910 claim that the tower "might collapse" was only a wire report at the time. Sources are in the references below.

Illustrations are AI-generated; historical figures are unnamed cartoon characters, not likenesses. Contracts, newspapers and council documents are not drawn, quotations appear on text cards, and modern researchers are not drawn.

Information as of 2026-10-20

ef101.text: In 1906, a Paris city council committee report posed a question:

ef102.text: This star attraction of the 1889 Exposition: keep it, or tear it down?

ef103.text: The report didn't answer; it said: our successors will decide in due time.

ef105.text: The tower was built under an 1887 contract, and that contract had a deadline;

ef106.text: That same year, famous names attacked it in the press; Eiffel's reply mentioned war;

ef107.text: later, someone sent a string of signals from it to the Panthéon, 4 km away;

ef108.text: later still, the War Ministry gave it a verdict: unique in the whole world;

ef109.text: and a wire report said its foundations flooded and it might fall.

ef110.text: People online say it was almost torn down in 1909. Is that true?

ef201.text: The contract was signed on January 8, 1887, by three parties:

ef202.text: Minister Lockroy for the State, Seine Prefect Poubelle for Paris, and Eiffel himself.

ef204.text: plus operating rights for the Exposition year and twenty years from January 1, 1890.

ef205.text: The tower itself? After the Exposition, it belonged to Paris;

ef206.text: at expiry, only the operating rights returned to Paris,

ef207.text: and he had to hand the tower back in good repair.

ef208.text: Did it say to tear it down at the end?

ef209.text: No. The State could demolish it only if Eiffel failed to finish it.

ef210.text: It did reserve a room on every level for scientific or military experiments.

ef211.text: Yet barely a month after signing, on February 14, the joint protest from the start ran in Le Temps;

ef212.text: nearly 50 artists and writers signed; Maupassant was one.

ef214.text: for twenty years its odious shadow would spread over the city like an ink blot.

ef215.text: They called it an odious column of bolted sheet iron,

ef218.text: First, he said it was too late: contracts signed, foundations laid.

ef219.text: Also, signer Garnier himself sat on the tower's review committee.

ef220.text: In the same paper, a reporter noted: what they opposed was the tower standing on after the Exposition.

ef221.text: Eiffel said: then the protest isn't too late, it's too early.

ef222.text: He said: I believe my tower will be beautiful; why would what's admired in Egypt become ugly and ridiculous in Paris?

ef223.text: He added: after the term, the city could do with it as it pleased.

ef224.text: Astronomy, meteorology, physics: scientists could all use it, he said;

ef225.text: and the war remark? His words: in wartime, it could keep Paris linked to the rest of France.

ef226.text: But after the Exposition, who would still pay to climb it?

ef301.text: Fewer and fewer. During the 1889 Exposition,

ef302.text: nearly 1.97 million paid visits reached the first floor;

ef303.text: by 1898, only a little over 183,000 a year.

ef304.text: So what did Eiffel use it for?

ef305.text: Experiments. Once it was built, the small 1.6-meter platform on top got weather instruments,

ef306.text: and cables sent the data to the weather bureau.

ef307.text: Remember those signals from the tower to the Panthéon?

ef308.text: On October 26, 1898, the signals were sent by a man named Ducretet.

ef309.text: 4 km apart, with tall buildings between: did the Panthéon receive them?

ef310.text: It did, always clearly, even in thick fog.

ef311.text: But from the Panthéon back to the tower, nothing got through.

ef312.text: On November 7, he put both results in a report to the French Academy of Sciences.

ef313.text: We think this was the first time the tower's height made its case.

ef314.text: From 1902, Eiffel also dropped objects from the tower to measure air resistance.

ef315.text: But the deadline drew closer each year. Did Paris mean to keep it or not?

ef401.text: Paris did ask. In 1903, the Seine Prefect wrote to the commission overseeing the tower:

ef402.text: When the contract expires, should the tower be kept, or demolished?

ef403.text: On October 10, the commission voted unanimously: keeping it had real benefits.

ef404.text: They said it was sound, and visitors were returning;

ef405.text: military too: the army was testing optical signals to Rouen and Fontainebleau;

ef406.text: and radio, the commission wrote, would add to that use later.

ef407.text: In 1906, the tower company itself applied to extend its operating rights.

ef408.text: Remember the report that left the decision to successors?

ef409.text: Its author said the Champ de Mars works would take years to finish;

ef410.text: but he also wrote that the many daily experiments on the tower were undeniably useful, and impressed him.

ef411.text: Its advice: until the successors decide, keep maintaining it and keep it open.

ef412.text: On July 12, the council first extended it five years, to 1915,

ef413.text: for 5,000 francs a year to the city plus a revenue share, and prompt repair of the faults the committee found.

ef414.text: By then, how far could the tower's radio reach?

ef415.text: Bizerte, 1,500 km away, could receive its telegrams;

ef416.text: in August 1907, reportedly even 1,700 km away, cruisers off Casablanca could receive it.

ef417.text: Then, in February 1908, the new radio station beside the tower burned down;

ef419.text: That year, the War Ministry wanted antennas hung straight from the top; Eiffel's wartime link was taken seriously.

ef420.text: What did that “unique in the whole world” mean?

ef421.text: It meant: given its shape and its place right by the Seine, it was the only antenna support of its kind in the world.

ef422.text: The army's permit was tied to the company's rights: the station would stay as long as they lasted.

ef423.text: On May 15, 1908, the rights were extended eleven more years, to 1926.

ef424.text: By 1909, the army's underground station was going in under the lawn, about 200 m from the tower;

ef425.text: that year, the Bureau of Longitudes had the tower send time signals twice a day.

ef427.text: So ships at sea could set clocks, find longitude.

ef428.text: Yet that August, a small-town US paper still claimed: it would likely come down in a few years.

ef429.text: The contract's original deadline was January 1, 1910. What would happen to the tower that day?

ef501.text: Nothing. Remember that eleven-year extension? By then it was no longer a deadline at all.

ef502.text: The 1909 claim from the start: the records we found show no plan, proposal or vote to demolish it;

ef503.text: the US paper's “coming down soon” was just a rumor.

ef504.text: The station below was due to start public time signals then.

ef505.text: But in late January 1910, the Seine flooded;

ef506.text: that's when the wire report saying it might fall went out.

ef508.text: The underground station: a sewer burst, the station flooded, and much equipment was damaged.

ef509.text: So when was the first time signal?

ef510.text: Not until May 23 did the tower's station send its first public time signal.

ef511.text: Remember those successors? They didn't tear it down; the rights kept being extended, all the way to 1980. File closed.

ef512.text: Where did you first hear the demolition story?

ef513.text: We tell only what the records show; subscribe to open files with us.
